title: CRA Classification Self-Check
intro: A few quick questions, about two minutes. You'll get an indicative CRA classification, your route to the CE marking, your specific gaps and a readiness score — grounded in the regulation, not a vendor pitch. Then submit it to OXOT for a human review and a call.
disclaimer: This is an indicative read, not a legal determination. OXOT confirms your classification with you in the intake. Grounded in Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 (the Cyber Resilience Act) and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392, which fixes the technical scope of Important (Annex III) and Critical (Annex IV) products.
scarcityNote: 2026 reality: zero notified bodies · Class I self-assessment needs harmonised standards or common specifications (none yet; ~Q2 2027) · designation takes 12–18 months. The queue forms before the doors open.

options.label: Product manufacturer
options.insight: As the manufacturer you carry the full weight of the CRA — the Annex VII technical file, the CE marking, and from 11 September 2026 a 24-hour early warning for actively exploited vulnerabilities.

options.label: OEM — multiple product groups
options.insight: The portfolio math is unforgiving: at 16–24 weeks per product type-examination, a large catalogue doesn't fit before 11 Dec 2027. Module H (one audited quality-management system) is usually the only way through — and it takes 8–14 months to stand up.

options.label: Integrator / systems integrator
options.insight: Watch Article 22: a substantial modification — your own firmware, changed security properties — makes YOU the manufacturer of the modified product. Configuring is fine; building is not. Most integrators can't yet say which side of that line their projects sit on.

options.label: Distributor / reseller
options.insight: From 11 Dec 2027 you may only offer CRA-compliant products, and you must verify the CE marking and declaration of conformity on each. Rebrand a line, and Article 21 makes you its manufacturer — full technical file included.

options.label: Owner / operator (procurement)
options.insight: Your practical CRA exposure isn't your own compliance — it's your suppliers'. NIS2 already asks your estate for state-of-the-art; the CRA raises the bar on every product entering it. 2026 is the year to test suppliers, while you can still switch.

questions.label: Does your product include software, or connect to a network or another device?

options.label: Yes
options.insight: Then you're in scope. The CRA covers all 'products with digital elements' — anything with software or a direct or indirect logical/physical connection to a device or network.

options.label: No
options.insight: You may be out of scope — the CRA covers products with digital elements. But 'likely out' is not 'certainly out', and a wrong call here is expensive; confirm it.

options.label: Not sure
options.insight: If it has any software or connectivity, assume in-scope until proven otherwise — the definition is deliberately broad, and it reaches components, not just finished products.

questions.label: Which comes closest to your product?

options.label: A general product with digital elements (e.g. a connected sensor or appliance)
options.insight: Default products self-assess (Module A) — but 'self-assess' still means a full Annex VII technical file, an SBOM and a vulnerability-handling process, all audit-ready by the deadline.

options.label: A security-relevant function (password/identity manager, VPN, firewall, network management, SIEM, boot manager)
options.insight: Class I can self-assess only against harmonised standards or common specifications (Art. 32(2)) — and neither exists yet (expected ~Q2 2027). Until one lands the self-route is shut; the alternative runs through a notified body, of which zero are designated today.

options.label: A core security or OT component (HSM, secure element, industrial firewall, PLC/RTU/DCS, safety controller, smart-meter gateway)
options.insight: Class II requires third-party assessment outright — Module B+C or a full Module H quality-management system. There is no self-assessment route, and capacity — not effort — is the binding constraint.

options.label: A critical component (smart meter, smartcard, hardware device with a security box, used by essential entities)
options.insight: Critical products face mandatory third-party assessment and may require European cybersecurity certification — the tightest and longest route. Classification and capacity planning should start immediately.

options.label: Not sure
options.insight: Classification is the single highest-leverage decision under the CRA — it sets your entire route. Getting a confident read is exactly what the 45-minute intake does, live.

questions.label: Do you rebrand, substantially modify, or add your own firmware to another vendor's product?

options.label: Yes
options.insight: That likely reclassifies you as the manufacturer under Articles 21/22 — with the full technical file, a PSIRT/vulnerability-handling process, and the reporting duties that follow. This is the trap most integrators and distributors miss.

options.label: No
options.insight: Good — pure configuration and distribution keep you out of manufacturer status. But keep the line bright: the moment you change security properties, the obligations move to you.

questions.label: Are the products placed on the EU market (directly or via distributors)?

options.label: Yes
options.insight: EU market access is now conditional on CRA conformity — after 11 Dec 2027 a non-compliant product cannot be placed on, or made available in, the EU market. The clock is already running.

options.label: No / not yet
options.insight: If you sell into the EU indirectly — via distributors or as a component in someone else's product — the obligations still reach you. Worth confirming your real exposure.

questions.label: Which do you already have, per product? (this sets your gaps)

on_track.title: On track
on_track.note: You hold the core artifacts. The work now is routing and sequencing against the deadline.

behind.title: Behind
behind.note: You're missing a core artifact. Recoverable — but the queue for third-party capacity is forming now.

at_risk.title: At risk
at_risk.note: Gaps plus a route that can't self-assess today. This is the profile that runs out of runway before 11 Dec 2027.

gaps.label: Your gaps
gaps.none: You already hold the SBOM, risk assessment and vulnerability-handling process — the review is about routing and sequencing, not starting from zero.

items.sbom: No SBOM yet — it's the foundation of the Annex VII file and the first thing an assessor asks for.
items.risk: No risk assessment — Annex I requires it, and it drives the whole security design and your residual-risk case.
items.cvd: No coordinated vulnerability disclosure / PSIRT — mandatory, and it's what turns 24-hour incident reporting from panic into process.

CLASS_I.headline: Likely Important, Class I — and the self-assessment door is currently closed.
CLASS_I.body: Class I products can't self-certify until harmonised CRA standards are designated (expected ~Q2 2027). Every external route runs through a notified body — and today zero are designated. The wall is fixed at 11 December 2027. The queue is forming now.
CLASS_I.route: Route: third-party assessment — self-assessment needs harmonised standards or common specifications (Art. 32(2)); neither exists yet.

CLASS_II.headline: Likely Important, Class II — third-party assessment is mandatory.
CLASS_II.body: Class II products require conformity assessment by a notified body — Module B+C, or a full Module H quality-management system. With effectively zero bodies designated in 2026, capacity, not effort, is your binding constraint.
CLASS_II.route: Route: Module B+C or Module H (third-party).

CRITICAL.headline: Likely Critical — the tightest route, and possibly EU certification.
CRITICAL.body: Critical products face mandatory third-party assessment and may require European cybersecurity certification. Classification and capacity planning should start immediately — this is the longest path to the CE marking.
CRITICAL.route: Route: third-party assessment (+ possible EU certification).

DEFAULT.headline: Likely a default product with digital elements.
DEFAULT.body: You can self-assess (Module A) in principle — but you still owe a full Annex VII technical file, an SBOM and a vulnerability-handling process, all audit-ready by 11 December 2027. 'Self-assess' is not 'do less'.
DEFAULT.route: Route: self-assessment (Module A) — the technical file is still required.

NEEDS_REVIEW.headline: Your class needs a proper read.
NEEDS_REVIEW.body: From these answers we can't place your product with confidence — which is common, and exactly what the 45-minute intake resolves, live, with an OT engineer.
NEEDS_REVIEW.route: Route: to be determined at intake.

OUT_OF_SCOPE_LIKELY.headline: Likely out of scope — but confirm it.
OUT_OF_SCOPE_LIKELY.body: The CRA covers products with digital elements. If none of yours have software or connectivity, you may be out of scope — but 'likely' is not 'certainly', and a wrong call here is expensive.

s7Callout.text: A Siemens S7-1500 in an energy utility = Class II. The same device in a food packaging plant = likely Class I.

v2.reportingClock: Your first hard date is not Dec 2027 — it is 11 September 2026: 24h early warning, 72h notification, 14d final report to ENISA.
v2.programmeStrip: Classify → Test → File. From about €20K. Phase 1 typically 2–4 weeks per product. Vincent replies within 2 days.

runway.title: Can you make the wall?
annotations: Serial testing: 16–24 weeks per product, one after another.
Module H parallelises the queue — one audited quality system covers the whole portfolio, but takes 8–14 months to stand up.
